title: Global AI Trade Unwind Drives Foreign Investors Back to Indian Equities
excerpt: After selling $29 billion in the first half of 2026, foreign investors turned net buyers of Indian stocks in July as a pullback in AI-linked markets triggered a major rotation into India's diversified benchmarks.
body:
• Foreign investors bought $1.6 billion of Indian equities in July after selling $29 billion in H1 2026, marking a sharp reversal in flows.
  • The Nifty IT index surged 16.8% in July — its strongest monthly gain in six years — as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 21%.
  • HSBC, UBS, Goldman Sachs and Bernstein have all upgraded or flagged bullish outlooks on Indian markets for the second half of 2026.

Indian equities posted consecutive monthly gains for the first time this year in July, powered by an unwinding of the global AI trade that sent foreign capital rushing back into one of the markets worst hit by the AI-driven outflow cycle.

The Nifty 50 rose 2.2% and the Sensex gained 2.1% in July, according to Reuters. The rally was led by a 16.8% surge in the Nifty IT index — its strongest monthly showing in six years — as beaten-down software exporters attracted investors fleeing AI-linked positions in South Korea, Taiwan, and the United States.

The Great Rotation

The numbers tell a stark reversal story. Foreign investors, who sold $29.3 billion of Indian equities in the first six months of 2026, turned net buyers in July, bringing in $1.6 billion. While modest in absolute terms, the shift represents a dramatic change in direction after months of relentless selling.

"The shift from AI-driven frenzy to more broad-based earnings growth in India has attracted global investors, adding another layer of strength to domestic markets."

— Gaurav Didwania, Fund Manager, Qode

The catalyst: a pullback in AI-related shares that rattled the semiconductor-heavy markets that had dominated global flows. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 21% in July, South Korea's technology-heavy index plunged 24%, and Taiwan's equity benchmark dropped 7%. The Nifty IT index's outperformance versus U.S. chipmakers was the widest for any month since 1999, according to a Goldman Sachs note dated July 29.

Todd McClone, portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which oversees about $65 billion, said India had emerged as the "obvious destination" for investors trimming North Asian and U.S. technology exposure. His fund started turning positive on India in April and added positions in June after the Reserve Bank of India took steps to support the rupee.

Upgrades Pile Up

The institutional endorsements are stacking up. HSBC upgraded India to "neutral" from "underweight" over the past month, while UBS lifted its rating to "attractive" from "neutral." Goldman Sachs and Bernstein have both flagged the prospect of a second-half rebound for the Nifty 50.

Amundi, which manages $2.8 trillion in assets, said it was "constructive" on India. Ji Young Park, Amundi's senior Asia ex-Japan equity portfolio manager, said concerns over high oil prices were now largely reflected in valuations. She expects AI-driven rotation into India to persist as valuations in financials, healthcare, and industrials have become attractive — though she cautioned the IT rally could face headwinds from uncertain earnings amid AI-led disruption.

Individual stocks reflected the broader trend. HCLTech surged 25.7% in July after beating quarterly estimates and approving fresh investment in an Indian AI data centre. Infosys, TCS, and Tech Mahindra climbed between 12.9% and 17.6%. Bajaj Finance rallied 8.3% and Mahindra & Mahindra rose 3.5% on strong earnings.

India as the Anti-AI Trade

For much of the past year, India was viewed as the "anti-AI trade" by global investors, according to Outlook Business. While semiconductor-driven markets surged on AI optimism, Indian equities struggled with expensive valuations and the absence of listed companies directly benefiting from the AI hardware boom. That very weakness is now proving a strength.

A DSP Netra report found that around 72% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index's gains this year came from just three semiconductor companies — TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix — which now account for roughly 30% of the benchmark. That concentration leaves the index exposed to any cooling in AI sentiment, while India, trading near its long-term valuation average, offers diversification.

Brent crude hovering around $70 per barrel has provided additional tailwind. As one of the world's largest crude importers, India benefits through reduced inflation, an improving current account deficit, and stronger corporate profitability.

Diaspora Investors Watch Closely

For NRI investors with exposure to both U.S. technology stocks and Indian equities, the rotation raises portfolio allocation questions. Those who held Indian positions through the downturn are now seeing recovery, while the AI pullback may dent portfolios tilted toward U.S. tech. Indian corporate earnings are projected to grow at around 16% CAGR over FY26-FY28, compared with roughly 7% over the previous two years, according to Livemint.

What's Next

Whether the inflows prove durable depends on two factors, analysts said: a sustained recovery in Indian corporate earnings after several lackluster quarters, and a de-escalation of tensions in the Middle East that have kept crude prices volatile.

"India is set up for a strong second half of the year."

— Todd McClone, Portfolio Manager, William Blair

Mayuresh Joshi, head of equity research at William O'Neil & Company, said India could emerge as "one of the few markets where growth remains sustainable compared with the rest of the world." Most analysts, however, characterize the move as portfolio rotation rather than the start of a new market regime — the structural AI investment story remains intact, but capital is broadening beyond a handful of semiconductor winners toward economies with more balanced growth profiles.
nri_angle: NRI investors with portfolios spanning U.S. tech and Indian equities face rebalancing decisions as the AI-to-India rotation reshapes global flows.
author: Diaspora Desk
